messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 50
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Musician
  trauma_type: Stalking
  pcl5: 45

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Threat: Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Watching Others: I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me, Night Vigilance: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day
  Memory: Memory Gaps: There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try, Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once, Sudden Pieces: Fragments of the memory appear suddenly without warning and then disappear
  Negative Appraisals: Emotional Numbness: I feel dead inside, Weakness Belief: I am a weak person, Institutional Failure: The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Minh, a 50-year-old divorced Vietnamese American musician, described the stalking as beginning almost imperceptibly, with a woman who first appeared at small club performances, lingering near the back wall and waiting outside after sets. At first he tried to be polite, then to ignore her, but over weeks her calls multiplied, she learned the names of his former bandmates, and one night he found notes slipped beneath the windshield wiper of his car. What finally made the situation feel unbearable was the sense that the people he expected to help could not or would not: when he reported the messages and the repeated appearances, he felt dismissed, told there was not enough to act on. Minh had come to believe that he was weak for not stopping it himself, and that the institutions that should have protected him had let him down. Those beliefs sat heavily with him, leaving him feeling dead inside and oddly ashamed of how much the stalking had shaken him.

After that, Minh began organizing his life around danger. He avoided unfamiliar places because he could not assess who might be waiting there, and he grew vigilant with everyone around him, watching faces, hands, and exits for any sign that someone meant him harm. Night was worst; in the dark he felt stripped of whatever small sense of control he could hold onto during the day. He started choosing only familiar streets to drive home from gigs, and if a show ended late he would ask another musician to walk him to his car. Even the ordinary business of playing music changed: he stopped taking last-minute gigs in clubs he did not know, because the prospect of an unrecognized parking lot or a dim alley felt too risky. His divorce, already painful, became another place where he felt he had failed to hold his life together, and that sense of weakness made the world seem even less predictable.

The more Minh watched for danger, the more his mind seemed to hand him pieces of the stalking without warning. A fragment of a voice, a glimpse of a figure near a doorway, the sudden sight of a note-like scrap of paper could pull him back so completely that the memory felt real across all his senses at once: the smell of cold air outside a venue, the scrape of shoes on concrete, the sick lurch in his stomach as he realized he was being tracked. Other parts of it remained blank no matter how hard he tried to recall them, and those gaps troubled him because they made him feel as if he had somehow failed to understand what had happened. When the memory arrived in those abrupt fragments, it confirmed for him that he had been powerless to keep the situation under control, and that sense of powerlessness fed the belief that he was weak. In turn, feeling weak made him search the environment even more intensely, as though alertness might prevent the next intrusion.

The cycle tightened in the months that followed. Minh’s threat monitoring became so constant that memory intrusions seemed to come more easily; once he had spent an evening scanning the audience at a bar in fear of seeing someone who resembled the woman, the image of her standing outside his car would return later that night, vivid and complete. He would then feel again that the world had not protected him, and that he himself had not been strong enough to make anyone take it seriously. Those thoughts deepened his numbness and sharpened his sense that he must keep watching, because if he relaxed even briefly, something else could happen. He found himself checking unfamiliar people more carefully than he wanted to, and when he was alone after a performance he often sat in his car longer than necessary, staring through the windshield before driving away. At home, he kept more lights on at night and slept lightly, uneasy in the dark.

By the time he sought help, Minh was exhausted by his own vigilance and embarrassed by how much his world had shrunk. He had stopped accepting some invitations to play, especially in neighborhoods he did not know, and he worried that his work as a musician was becoming defined by fear rather than skill. What brought him in now was the realization that he was still living as if the stalking were about to resume at any moment, and that the sudden flashes of memory and the constant scanning were no longer letting him rest. He hoped for relief from the feeling of being dead inside, but what frightened him most was that he might always remain the kind of man who could be made to feel weak and unprotected by a threat that had never fully gone away.
